Rejected Alternatives

Keep distributed decisions with local fixes

Local timeout conditions, application-side rescans, and generic wakeup booleans can address individual failures but retain multiple decision authorities. They cannot consistently preserve reason and publication ordering.

Let the reactor infer whether a manager can make progress from a raw delay

A raw zero delay is ambiguous: it can mean executable work is ready, or that a local timer is overdue while another condition still prevents progress. Making the reactor interpret heartbeat, commit, fetch, metadata, and share acknowledgement state would duplicate manager rules in the shared kernel. The constrained PollResult shapes instead require each manager to classify its own result and let the reactor validate only the generic no-progress invariant. WAIT_FOREVER already removes one manager's timer, but it does not identify the enabling input or keep work admission and wait calculation on one state projection. Local guards remain necessary; the typed result makes their outcome observable to scheduling and liveness tests.

Add a generic readiness kernel or signal registry

The existing reactor already receives application inputs, network completions, cancellation, and shutdown wakeups. A second signal registry would duplicate those channels and add lifecycle, boundedness, and missed-signal questions. The minimal rule is local: a manager derives one activation projection and reports its result with NextPollCondition. New readiness infrastructure is justified only if a later manager demonstrates a dependency that the existing input paths and stable ordered pass cannot express.

Put all consumer logic in one reactor class

This centralizes code rather than decisions and would mix regular/share behavior into the execution kernel. Managers and drivers keep their rules local while the reactor remains the final coordination boundary.

Implement separate regular and share reactor stacks

Duplicating queue drain, scheduling, publication, shutdown, and action ordering invites different concurrency bugs. The consumers share the kernel but not their state machines.

Migrate all managers in one patch

An all-at-once rewrite removes comparison seams and makes regressions difficult to localize. The phased approach keeps each slice runnable and independently testable.

Traverse a dynamic manager dependency graph

The configured request-manager list is small and fixed for one consumer instance. A stable full ordered pass before each network poll is the correctness baseline and has O(active managers) cost. If measurement later justifies incremental polling, the protocol driver may own a static fact-type-to-manager index and poll a stable dirty set. Recursive polling, fixed-point evaluation, and a dynamic dependency DAG are non-goals.

Replay transport work after a pre-I/O cross-owner fact

Replaying or cancelling requests already built in the same pre-I/O pass would require dependency metadata for every command, a definition of which manager state may be replayed, and new duplicate-attempt semantics. The simpler invariant prevents that state: cross-owner facts enter through input or network-completion paths, before the next full manager pass builds transport work. The POC's pre-I/O containment remains diagnostic support for migration errors, not a second target execution model.

Related Work

  • KAFKA-14246 and the consumer threading refactor design deliberately introduced an event-driven communication boundary between the application and network threads. That design did not attempt to model all same-thread request-manager coordination as events, so cross-manager progress, lifecycle, scheduling, and application-visible effect decisions could remain distributed across managers and completion paths. This KIP builds on that topology by defining ConsumerReactor as the background-thread orchestrator and by making cross-manager ordering, state ownership, schedule publication, and action ordering explicit; it does not reject or replace the original refactor.
  • KIP-945 is a WIP proposal documenting the broader threading-model intent. It remains related history, not this KIP's baseline or a prerequisite.
  • KAFKA-20854 / PR #23014 fixes a fetch wake/effect-classification bug. It motivates typed manager output and effect ordering, but is not evidence that the numeric wait field caused every busy loop.

version_bodies.title: KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers

version.message: Narrow KIP-1371 to explicit wait conditions for consumer request managers

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Draft

Discussion thread: TBD

JIRA: KAFKA-20995

Release: TBD

Summary

The async consumer has repeatedly entered busy loops when a request-manager timer reports zero while a prerequisite prevents the corresponding work from progressing. The network and application wait projections have both exhibited this failure shape. This KIP applies the resulting programming-model change to network-thread scheduling.

Consumer request managers decide both what work to perform and how long the network thread may wait before another iteration. Those decisions depend on related state: a heartbeat timer can expire while the previous request is still in flight, and a blocked request can still have an independent operation expiry. Numeric waits can represent the correct result, while the combined value hides the prerequisite that selected or suppressed a deadline.

This KIP proposes one owner-local result for execution and scheduling, represented through named, composable wait conditions. Each poll() returns its outgoing requests together with the condition for the next manager pass. Request managers express immediate work, deadlines, and the absence of a deadline through ready(), after(...), and idle(). Owners express prerequisites with ordinary if branches; either(...) combines independent obligations. The network thread polls every manager once for work, aggregates the returned conditions, and uses the earliest manager or transport deadline to bound network I/O. The existing application-wait projection is evaluated separately.

The intended benefit is a programming model whose waiting intent and prerequisite relationships are easier to read, review, and maintain. One shared owner decision keeps send admission and scheduling aligned. Request-state objects expose that decision as a condition: request admission uses isReady(...), while the manager returns the same condition for network scheduling. The existing duration interface can represent the same waits; its API does not require owners to expose one executable decision for both uses.

This shared decision governs network-thread admission and next-pass scheduling. The existing internal maximumTimeToWait(...) application projection becomes applicationPollCondition(...) and uses the same condition vocabulary, while its policy, aggregation, and published cachedMaximumTimeToWait duration remain separate. The KIP does not merge the network and application timing policies.

The proposal preserves the existing deadline-driven network loop, thread topology, manager order, input wakeups, public APIs, configuration, and protocols. Performance serves as an acceptance constraint. Current measurements leave idle CPU behavior and throughput non-regression open for validation.

Motivation

Today, RequestManager.poll(long currentTimeMs) performs local work and returns outgoing requests together with PollResult.timeUntilNextPollMs. The network thread polls all managers and bounds its network wait by the minimum returned duration and its existing poll cap. Zero requests an immediate iteration; a finite duration requests a timed iteration; Long.MAX_VALUE contributes no deadline. A manager is still polled on an iteration caused by another manager or input.

There is a separate application-wait interface, currently maximumTimeToWait(long). Its aggregate is published as cachedMaximumTimeToWait for application-thread waiting. The proposal changes the internal per-manager return type to applicationPollCondition(long) so the same explicit conditions can represent application waits. The existing application-wait policy and the published duration remain unchanged and are not combined with network scheduling.

Recurring busy loops across request-manager wait projections

Several consumer busy-loop fixes share one failure shape: a local timer is due, the operation cannot make progress, and the manager still contributes a zero wait. The affected network or application loop immediately starts another iteration and reaches the same answer.

EvidenceStatus as of 2026-09-21Affected projectionWork blocked bySource of the zero waitRepair
PR #22836 — KAFKA-20253: Heartbeat CPU spin fix for Consumer protocolMergedNetwork scheduling for in-flight coordinator discovery; application wait for heartbeat and auto-commit.Coordinator discovery or heartbeat progress is waiting on coordinator/request state.An elapsed retry or heartbeat timer remains urgent while the related operation cannot advance.Withdraw the in-flight coordinator deadline; use heartbeat or auto-commit intervals on affected application-wait paths.
PR #23227 — KAFKA-20970: Another busy loop happens if auto.commit.interval.ms is less than bootstrap.resolve.timeout.msMergedApplication waitAuto-commit is waiting for coordinator discovery during bootstrap DNS resolution.The auto-commit timer has expired, so the application wait remains zero.Use the auto-commit interval while the coordinator is unavailable; apply a similar heartbeat-interval guard to Streams.
PR #23348 — KAFKA-21010: Another busy loop happens if the member is in JOINING state and bootstrap DNS resolution is not finishedMergedApplication waitHeartbeat is waiting for coordinator discovery.The initial heartbeat interval is zero while the coordinator remains unknown.Replace zero-capable heartbeat and auto-commit interval substitutes with the retry backoff and refine terminal-state guards.
PR #23357 — KAFKA-21031: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expiredOpenNetwork scheduling and application waitA heartbeat response is still in flight.The expired heartbeat timer contributes zero even though another heartbeat cannot be sent.Use the initial retry backoff with a one-millisecond floor because retry backoff also accepts zero.

These repairs correctly fix their individual paths. The direct network-scheduling evidence is the in-flight coordinator path in PR #22836 and the in-flight heartbeat path in PR #23357. The application-wait fixes demonstrate the same timer-substitution hazard in the separate compatibility projection, which this KIP leaves unchanged. Across both projections, a new manager state can block request creation while leaving a separately calculated timer eligible to drive a loop.

The recurring relationship is:

  • a work source's timer contributes urgency only while that work's prerequisites allow progress;
  • an independent expiry remains relevant even while sending is blocked; and
  • after a terminal action, the owner must remove or update the obligation that made it urgent.

Substituting another timeout makes correctness configuration-dependent

The application-wait fixes show the limits of replacing an inapplicable zero deadline with another positive duration. PR #22836 used the heartbeat or auto-commit interval, and PR #23227 used the auto-commit interval for an unavailable coordinator. Those substitutions stop an immediate loop only while the selected interval is positive. PR #23348 subsequently replaced them with the retry backoff because the heartbeat interval is zero until the first heartbeat response and the auto-commit interval may also be configured as zero. PR #23357 encountered the same choice on the network path, found that retry backoff also accepts zero, and proposed a one-millisecond floor for the in-flight heartbeat case.

Each change addresses the observed state, but the sequence moves the safety requirement from one duration to another. A timer setting then determines whether blocked work spins, how frequently it is rechecked, and how quickly it recovers if the expected wakeup is delayed. The enabling event is unchanged: an in-flight request needs a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout; an unavailable coordinator needs coordinator discovery. Passage of a heartbeat, auto-commit, or retry interval does not satisfy those prerequisites.

The network-scheduling model therefore applies work eligibility before configuration-derived timing. A blocked manager work source withdraws its deadline for every timer value. Independent manager and transport expiries keep their own deadlines. This property depends on the owner selecting the correct condition; the condition type makes the rule explicit and reusable without inferring domain eligibility itself.

For example, heartbeat scheduling must preserve the max.poll.interval.ms expiry even while an in-flight heartbeat blocks another send. The current duration model can represent that relationship:

Math.min(pollTimeoutRemainingMs,
    canSendHeartbeat ? heartbeatRemainingMs : Long.MAX_VALUE);

Correctness depends on applying the same canSendHeartbeat prerequisite in both request admission and wait calculation while retaining the independent poll timeout. The returned number records only the final duration; the selecting obligation and suppressed prerequisite remain implicit. Reviewers must reconstruct those relationships from surrounding branches and state, and each new state combination creates another opportunity for the two decisions to diverge.

Public Interfaces

Public consumer classes, metrics, configuration, wire protocols, persisted data, and broker behavior remain unchanged. ManagerPollCondition and the changes to PollResult remain internal to org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.

Proposed Changes

1. Return work and the next wait condition from one poll

Extend the internal PollResult returned by RequestManager.poll(...):

final class PollResult {
    List<UnsentRequest> unsentRequests;
    ManagerPollCondition nextPollCondition;
}

The existing PollResult(List<UnsentRequest>) and PollResult(UnsentRequest) constructors remain as adapters for unconditional close and drain paths and for internal helpers whose enclosing manager replaces the condition before returning. Those constructors contribute idle() after staging their request because the next useful input is normally its network completion. They can be removed once those paths state their post-action condition explicitly.

The result is one atomic owner-local outcome: work produced in this pass and the condition for the following pass. Existing queues and wakeups carry inputs, and the ordered manager pass remains the execution mechanism.

FormMeaningNetwork-wait contribution
ready()Another iteration can perform a local step immediately.Zero
after(now, delayMs)Re-evaluate by the absolute deadline computed from the supplied remaining delay.Remaining time to that deadline
idle()This work source withdraws its autonomous deadline.Long.MAX_VALUE

An owner selects idle() when a prerequisite blocks a work source, before consulting that work source's timer. ready() and after(...) apply only after the work becomes eligible. This ordering gives the condition a configuration-independent property:

work source blocked by a prerequisite
    -> idle(), for every configured timer value

work source eligible
    -> ready() or after(...), according to its timer

idle() applies to one manager work source; it does not request an unbounded selector wait. An independent expiry is composed separately with either(...), so suppressing an in-flight heartbeat deadline does not suppress max.poll.interval.ms expiry or other local work. Network response, disconnect, cancellation, shutdown, and application-event paths activate the loop when blocked state changes.

Transport contributes a separate deadline for the earliest request timeout. It is the minimum of unsent-request timers retained by NetworkClientDelegate and requests already sent by NetworkClient. A sent-request deadline derives from actual send time, per-request timeout, and accumulated throttle time. Kafka currently bounds each selector wait by the full default request timeout and, while unsent requests exist, by the existing delegate retry-backoff cap. The proposal preserves both bounds and adds the earliest remaining unsent-or-sent request deadline.

InFlightRequests expires a request when elapsed time minus throttle is strictly greater than its timeout, so the derived deadline includes the following millisecond. Throttle learned from another response may move the deadline later; an early wake is safe and recomputes the conservative deadline. The final network wait is the minimum of the manager aggregate, transport deadline, metadata and telemetry deadlines, and the existing global network-poll cap. This keeps a blocked manager source at idle() without delaying unsent or sent request-timeout detection to the global cap.

Exposing the sent-request deadline requires an internal query on KafkaClient, implemented by NetworkClient and its test or alternate implementations. The exact helper placement remains an implementation detail, while the unsent-plus-sent minimum and timeout semantics are required behavior. This transport contribution must be complete before the implementation is merged. The current prototype already returns idle() for in-flight request state and temporarily relies on the five-second network-poll cap.

A local step may produce a request, propagate an error, expire an operation, or advance a state transition. ready() marks any such step as immediately due, including local-only work. idle() withdraws the work source's autonomous deadline while the manager remains part of every ordered pass. Completion and enabling-input identity remain in owner state. Existing application-event wakeups and network response, disconnect, and timeout processing supply inputs that change that state.

either(first, second) combines independent obligations. Its remaining wait is the minimum of the inputs; isReady(now) is true when either input is ready. This composition operation applies to the three waiting forms above.

Owners use ordinary if branches to check prerequisites and select a condition for each work source. Independent expiry is then combined with that condition. This keeps branch policy visible in the owner while centralizing deadline composition.

For request sources using RequestState, the state object provides the common decision directly:

ManagerPollCondition sendCondition(long now) {
    if (requestInFlight())
        return ManagerPollCondition.idle();
    long remainingBackoffMs = remainingBackoffMs(now);
    return remainingBackoffMs <= 0
        ? ManagerPollCondition.ready()
        : ManagerPollCondition.after(now, remainingBackoffMs);
}

boolean canSendRequest(long now) {
    return sendCondition(now).isReady(now);
}

A request manager returns this same condition when it produces no request. Once it sends, onSendAttempt(...) changes the request state and the post-action condition becomes idle(). A response or failure clears the in-flight state and restores the applicable backoff condition. This arrangement gives admission and scheduling one implementation of the in-flight prerequisite that was previously easy to encode in only one path.

remainingMs(now) converts a condition to a network-wait bound. isReady(now) identifies an immediate or elapsed condition and can be used for a particular owner-local action. Request admission uses the condition for that specific action. Only an action-specific condition authorizes its action. An aggregate represents urgency across actions: either(operationExpiry, heartbeatSendCondition).isReady(now) may be true because expiry needs processing while sending remains blocked. A timer contributes readiness only after applying the owner's prerequisites.

after uses Kafka's Time.milliseconds() clock domain, rejects negative delays, and uses saturating addition to avoid overflow. Zero delay remains legal. The owner supplies the remaining budget from a retained timer, preserving the original deadline across iterations.

The revised loop has the following shape. This is illustrative pseudocode; exception handling, resource initialization, and shutdown retain their existing paths.

void runOnce() {
    processApplicationEvents();
    long iterationStartMs = time.milliseconds();

    ManagerPollCondition nextPoll = ManagerPollCondition.after(
        iterationStartMs, MAX_POLL_TIMEOUT_MS);
    for (RequestManager manager : requestManagers) {
        NetworkClientDelegate.PollResult result =
            manager.poll(time.milliseconds());
        networkClientDelegate.addAll(result);
        nextPoll = ManagerPollCondition.either(
            nextPoll, result.nextPollCondition());
    }

    long now = time.milliseconds();
    long transportWaitMs =
        networkClientDelegate.timeToNextTransportTimeoutMs(now);
    networkClientDelegate.poll(
        Math.min(nextPoll.remainingMs(now), transportWaitMs), now);
    updateCachedMaximumTimeToWait();
    reapExpiredApplicationEvents();
    propagateMetadataErrors();
}

Every manager keeps its existing execution opportunity. Its result describes the state left by that execution. When a manager transition makes another manager urgent, the transitioning manager can return ready() to request the next ordered pass. Inputs processed by network I/O become visible on the following manager pass. The loop keeps its existing bounded iteration model.

The existing five-second network-poll cap is retained, anchored at the start of the manager pass and reduced by elapsed processing time. applicationPollCondition(long) remains a separate application-wait projection whose aggregate is lowered to the existing duration publication; pollOnClose(long) remains unconditional. After all internal callers migrate, PollResult carries outgoing requests and ManagerPollCondition without timeUntilNextPollMs or duration-only constructors.

2. Apply the model to existing scheduling cases

CaseExisting numeric expressionProposed expressionIntended benefit
Request in flight; local deadlines exhaustedLong.MAX_VALUE / PollResult.EMPTYidle()Name the withdrawal of timer urgency; behavior is already expressible today.
Retry backoff remainsRemaining backoff durationafter(now, remainingBackoffMs)Use common clock and deadline handling.
Local work can proceed immediatelyZero durationready()Make local-only urgency visible alongside RPC-producing work.
Request sending depends on a prerequisiteGuard choosing a duration or Long.MAX_VALUEif (canSend) selects the retry deadline; otherwise idle()Show which work source is restricted; use the same owner decision for sending and scheduling.
Blocked sending with an independent expiryMinimum of expiry and guarded send delayeither(operationExpiry, retryCondition)Make the independent obligation visible during review.
Multiple requests have different deadlinesMinimum over applicable durationseither(...) over applicable conditionsPreserve every applicable obligation in the composition.

Heartbeat applies the same rule with its additional interval and membership state. An in-flight heartbeat selects idle() before reading the heartbeat interval. Immediate join, acknowledgement, and leave heartbeats remain owner-local exceptions. Ordinary request admission and the returned scheduling condition consume the same heartbeat decision across regular, share, and Streams paths.

Coordinator discovery uses the generic RequestState.sendCondition(...) form. The result controls both whether FindCoordinator can be created and the condition returned with an empty result. An in-flight discovery therefore withdraws its expired backoff deadline in the same method that rejects a duplicate send. This is the failure shape behind the coordinator-discovery portion of KAFKA-20253.

The same request-state decision is reused by offset commit and fetch retries, topic-metadata retries, share acknowledgements, and Streams topology updates. Operation expiry remains a separate condition and is combined with request admission through either(...). Regular, share, and Streams heartbeats use an owner-local heartbeat condition because their admission also includes membership state and the heartbeat interval.

Fetch preparation and queued offset work already derive execution and scheduling from the same pending future or queue. Membership managers advance local state rather than admit a request through RequestState. Those owners return typed conditions without introducing another request-send abstraction.

The migration reuses owner-local decisions across execution and scheduling. Each work source with shared send prerequisites exposes that decision through a private helper or existing request-state abstraction. Managers retain distinct decisions for distinct actions: operation expiry and request sending have separate eligibility rules. Private helpers and existing request-state abstractions provide the required structure while preserving the current class hierarchy and callback model.

Independent expiry remains visible

An in-flight heartbeat suppresses urgency from its send timer. The independent max.poll.interval.ms deadline can still require the owner to initiate leaving, so that expiry remains outside the ordinary heartbeat guard. Starting the leave consumes that initiation deadline.

Likewise, metadata request A may await a response with 100 ms until expiry while request B can retry after 30 ms. The condition preserves both deadlines. The owner sends B when due, retains A's expiry, and removes terminal operations. either combines deadlines; the owner performs cleanup.

Limits of the mechanism

The owner selects idle() for a blocked work source, and either preserves an independently composed deadline. A missing prerequisite, incorrect ready(), or retained expired operation can still cause repeated zero waits. A misplaced guard can instead suppress necessary progress. Configured zero backoff can legitimately request successive immediate iterations.

The design makes these relationships explicit and reduces independently maintained decisions. Request managers continue to own policy, progress, and terminal cleanup. Focused tests verify their concrete state transitions and scheduling outcomes.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

The scope is the shared consumer network loop and request managers used by regular, share, and Streams consumer compositions. ClassicKafkaConsumer keeps its existing execution model. The consumer network-thread name, publication model, application-wait policy, published duration, and metrics remain unchanged. The internal per-manager application-wait method returns a typed condition after migration.

All request managers eventually return a typed condition in PollResult before the internal delay field is removed. The current prototype exercises every concrete request-manager type; owner-specific decisions continue to be consolidated where execution and scheduling share prerequisites. The internal migration proceeds in testable slices and preserves request eligibility, ordering, retry policy, operation deadlines, input wakeups, owner thread confinement, close-time work, and user-visible behavior.

Network-wait timing changes when a manager returns ready() after a transition that requires another ordered pass. Manager order and unconditional invocation remain unchanged. The processing-time-adjusted poll cap is retained. Recovery and queue policy remain outside this proposal.

Test Plan

Condition tests cover zero delay, idle, deadline expiry, overflow, composition, and a blocked work source with an independent expiry. Per-owner tests cover request eligibility and state-machine correctness.

For each migrated owner, focused tests check the condition returned with actual request production or local transitions. Cases include in-flight work, missing coordinator, backoff, independent expiry, successful completion, fatal error, and close. Repeated polls at fixed input state produce a positive or unbounded wait for work known to be blocked, then recover when its prerequisite changes. The same blocked state must select idle() with zero, positive, and maximum supported timer values. Legitimate immediate transitions and configured zero backoff remain explicit scheduling choices. A poll-timer expiry with an in-flight heartbeat must request immediate work only until the owner consumes the expiry by initiating the leave transition.

Network-loop tests check one work poll per manager, earliest-deadline aggregation, the separate application-wait query, unchanged application-wait publication, and unconditional close polling. In-flight tests verify that response, disconnect, cancellation, and request timeout reactivate processing while the manager condition is idle(). Transport tests verify the minimum of unsent and sent request deadlines, actual send time, accumulated throttle, the strict-expiry one-millisecond boundary, recomputation after an early wake, and the existing default-request-timeout bound. KafkaClient implementations and test fixtures cover the new internal query. Integration tests use real inputs and isolated broker/proxy fixtures to verify progress and deadlines.

Performance comparisons use a pinned baseline containing relevant fixes and a scope-isolated candidate. Measure active throughput, CPU and allocation, plus idle/blocked CPU and response latency. Performance acceptance requires a predeclared material-regression margin and stable measurement protocol; existing benchmark data remain preliminary. End-to-end results take precedence over reduced manager counts.

Documentation Plan

Internal Javadocs will define each condition, composition scope, clock handling, side-effect restrictions, and the distinction between network and application waiting. Contributor examples will show a shared owner decision and independent expiry. Existing public behavior keeps the documentation scope internal.

Rejected Alternatives

Retain the duration-only request-manager model

Request managers can continue returning a scalar duration and repair each busy loop with local guards or a substitute positive timeout. The related application-wait fixes and PR #23357 show that substitute heartbeat, auto-commit, and retry durations may themselves be zero or require an arbitrary floor. Their configured values then control blocked-state polling even though passage of those durations cannot satisfy the blocking prerequisite.

The proposal retains deadline-driven network polling while replacing the duration-only manager result with explicit conditions. A blocked work source withdraws its deadline through idle() for every timer configuration; eligible work uses ready() or after(...); independent deadlines compose through either(...).

Validation Status and Open Decisions

The prototype validates the core mechanics and exposes the remaining acceptance work. All production request-send admission paths now consume an action-specific condition also used for scheduling. Generic request state covers coordinator, commit, topic metadata, share acknowledgement, and Streams topology requests; owner-local helpers cover regular, share, and Streams heartbeats. Fetch, offsets, and membership keep their existing pending-work decisions because they have no separate request-send predicate to consolidate.

EvidenceWhat it supportsRemaining evidence
Focused heartbeat, state, condition, and scheduling testsPreservation of tested behavior, including an urgent heartbeat while another request is in flight and an independent poll expiryGeneral busy-loop coverage and performance acceptance
Commit scheduling regressionsExpired obligations must be removed and close scheduling must match work that close can processPer-owner cleanup validation
Executable comparison of guarded numeric and typed expressionsEquivalent scheduling results for the tested inputsBroader state coverage and reviewer usability feedback
Shared admission-condition migrationCoordinator, commit, topic metadata, share acknowledgement, Streams topology, and heartbeat paths use one action-specific decision for request admission and scheduling; focused suites preserve retry, in-flight, timeout, throttle, leave, and close behaviorZero, positive, and maximum timer-value sweep; reviewer usability feedback; stable performance comparison

The prototype currently returns idle() for in-flight request state while timeout detection still relies on the five-second network-poll cap. The required unsent-plus-sent transport deadline remains to be implemented and validated before merge. Performance acceptance also remains open; prior normal-idle measurements were inconclusive for CPU and showed increased allocation. Before implementation acceptance, validate the remaining end-to-end input and close paths and compare the typed implementation with an equivalent duration-based implementation under a stable performance protocol.

version_bodies.title: KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Draft

Discussion thread: TBD

JIRA: KAFKA-20995

Release: TBD

Summary

The async consumer has repeatedly entered busy loops when a timer reaches zero while another state blocks the related work. The current numeric wait says when to poll again, but it cannot say whether time can make the work eligible or another event must occur first. Existing fixes replace the zero with another duration, which can make correctness depend on that duration's configuration.

This KIP introduces the internal ManagerPollCondition type with ready(), after(...), and idle(). Each request-manager poll() returns its outgoing requests and the condition for the next manager pass. The same manager decision can govern request admission and network scheduling. The network thread combines all manager conditions and applies the existing network-poll bounds. Public APIs, protocols, and thread topology remain unchanged. The internal per-manager RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long) method becomes applicationPollCondition(long); the application-facing ApplicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait() path remains unchanged.

Motivation

The async consumer has repeatedly entered a busy loop when a timer reaches zero while another state prevents the related work from continuing. The loop polls the same request managers, gets the same zero wait, and immediately starts again.

Today, each request manager returns outgoing requests and one numeric wait. The network thread uses the minimum:

  for (RequestManager rm : requestManagers.entries()) {
    NetworkClientDelegate.PollResult pollResult = rm.poll(currentTimeMs);
    long timeoutMs = networkClientDelegate.addAll(pollResult);
    pollWaitTimeMs = Math.min(pollWaitTimeMs, timeoutMs);
}

0 starts another iteration immediately, a finite value schedules a timed iteration, and Long.MAX_VALUE adds no earlier deadline.

The application wait follows the same numeric model. Each manager returns a duration from RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long). The network thread publishes the minimum as cachedMaximumTimeToWait, and the application thread uses it to limit its wait.

Evidence from existing busy-loop fixes

The following issues share the same pattern: work is blocked, but its timer still contributes zero.

EvidenceStatus as of 2026-09-21Affected waitWork blocked bySource of zeroLocal repair
PR #22836 — KAFKA-20253: Heartbeat CPU spin fix for Consumer protocolMergedNetwork scheduling for in-flight coordinator discovery; application wait for heartbeat and auto-commit.Coordinator discovery or heartbeat progress is waiting on coordinator/request state.An elapsed retry or heartbeat timer remains urgent while the related operation cannot advance.Withdraw the in-flight coordinator deadline; use heartbeat or auto-commit intervals on affected application-wait paths.
PR #23227 — KAFKA-20970: Another busy loop happens if auto.commit.interval.ms is less than bootstrap.resolve.timeout.ms MergedApplication waitAuto-commit is waiting for coordinator discovery during bootstrap DNS resolution.The auto-commit timer has expired, so the application wait remains zero.Use the auto-commit interval while the coordinator is unavailable; apply a similar heartbeat-interval guard to Streams.
PR #23348 — KAFKA-21010: Another busy loop happens if the member is in JOINING state and bootstrap DNS resolution is not finishedMergedApplication waitHeartbeat is waiting for coordinator discovery.The initial heartbeat interval is zero while the coordinator remains unknown.Replace zero-capable heartbeat and auto-commit interval substitutes with the retry backoff and refine terminal-state guards.
PR #23357 — KAFKA-21031: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expiredOpenNetwork scheduling and application waitA heartbeat response is still in flight.The expired heartbeat timer contributes zero even though another heartbeat cannot be sent.Use the initial retry backoff with a one-millisecond floor because retry backoff also accepts zero.

Why the current timeout substitutions are incomplete

The fixes repair their reported paths by replacing one zero wait with another duration. PR #22836 and PR #23227 used heartbeat or auto-commit intervals. PR #23348 later used retry backoff because the heartbeat interval starts at zero and auto-commit may be configured as zero. PR #23357 found that retry backoff can also be zero and added a one-millisecond floor.

This approach has three drawbacks:

  • Correctness becomes configuration-dependent. A setting intended to control retry timing also decides whether blocked work enters a busy loop; configuring the replacement timer as zero restores the zero-wait loop.
  • A positive delay only postpones the next poll. Some prerequisites change when an event arrives: a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout resolves an in-flight request, while discovery supplies an unavailable coordinator. If none of these events has occurred, the next poll finds the manager still blocked.
  • A duration does not explain why the manager should run again. When backoff expires, the manager may send a request. When a request is in flight, the same elapsed time changes nothing; the manager still needs a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout.

The fixes remain correct for their reported cases, but they do not define one rule for future request-manager states.

Public Interfaces

Public consumer classes, metrics, configuration, wire protocols, persisted data, and broker behavior remain unchanged. ManagerPollCondition and the changes to PollResult remain internal to org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.

Proposed Changes

1. A request manager selects and returns its next poll condition

For the condition returned in PollResult, a request manager first checks whether its work can proceed:

  work blocked by a prerequisite
    -> idle()

work can proceed now
    -> ready()

time can make the work eligible
    -> after(now, delayMs)

For request sources using RequestState, one method supplies both request admission and network scheduling:

  ManagerPollCondition sendCondition(long now) {
    if (requestInFlight())
        return ManagerPollCondition.idle();

    long remainingBackoffMs = remainingBackoffMs(now);
    return remainingBackoffMs <= 0
        ? ManagerPollCondition.ready()
        : ManagerPollCondition.after(now, remainingBackoffMs);
}

boolean canSendRequest(long now) {
    return sendCondition(now).isReady(now);
}

A manager checks sendCondition(now).isReady(now) before creating a request. When no request is created, it returns that condition. After a send, onSendAttempt(...) changes the condition to idle() until a response or failure clears the in-flight state.

Each call to RequestManager.poll(now) answers two questions:

  1. What requests did this manager create in this pass?
  2. When can polling this manager again be useful?

PollResult carries both answers:

  final class PollResult {
    List<UnsentRequest> unsentRequests;
    ManagerPollCondition nextPollCondition;
}

The condition describes the manager state after producing the requests. For example, after a request is created and marked in flight, its next condition is normally idle() until the network response changes that state.

ManagerPollCondition has three forms:

FormMeaningWait returned by remainingMs(...)
ready()Another pass can perform work immediately.Zero
after(now, delayMs)Time can make another pass useful.Time remaining to the retained deadline
idle()This work has no local deadline.Long.MAX_VALUE

The internal API has this shape:

  interface ManagerPollCondition {
    boolean isReady(long currentTimeMs);
    long remainingMs(long currentTimeMs);

    static ManagerPollCondition ready() { ... }
    static ManagerPollCondition after(long currentTimeMs, long delayMs) { ... }
    static ManagerPollCondition idle() { ... }

    static ManagerPollCondition either(
        ManagerPollCondition first,
        ManagerPollCondition second
    ) { ... }
}

The implementation represents ready() and idle() as enum singletons:

  enum Constant implements ManagerPollCondition {
    READY,
    IDLE
}

either(first, second) is ready when either input is ready and retains the earlier wait. Therefore, either(ready(), x) is ready(), either(idle(), x) is x, and two timed conditions retain the earlier deadline instance. The implementation may return that instance directly to avoid allocating a composite.

after(...) rejects negative delays and retains one saturating absolute deadline. Zero delay is valid.

isReady(...) authorizes only the action whose condition was checked. A combined condition may be ready because another action expired while request sending remains blocked.

idle() removes only the deadline for this work. Other manager work, independent deadlines, network completions, application events, cancellation, and shutdown can still start another pass. For example, an in-flight heartbeat includes an idle() send condition and its independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry through either(...).

2. Apply the rule to current request managers

Manager stateReturned condition
A request is in flight.idle() for sending; keep independent operation expiry with either(...).
Retry backoff remains.after(now, remainingBackoffMs)

The following abridged runOnce() shows the scheduling change. The loop keeps the existing manager order and polls each manager once:

  void runOnce() {
    processApplicationEvents();
    final long currentTimeMs = time.milliseconds();

    ManagerPollCondition nextPoll =
        ManagerPollCondition.after(currentTimeMs, MAX_POLL_TIMEOUT_MS);

        long managerTimeMs = time.milliseconds();

            nextPoll, pollResult.nextPollCondition());
    }

    long networkPollWaitMs = nextPoll.remainingMs(networkPollTimeMs);

Current problemProposed behavior

The scope is the shared consumer network loop and request managers used by regular, share, and Streams consumers. ClassicKafkaConsumer keeps its existing execution model. Runtime thread names, metrics, application-wait behavior, configuration, protocols, and public consumer APIs remain unchanged.

Every request manager returns ManagerPollCondition in PollResult. Manager order, retry rules, operation deadlines, close behavior, and existing wakeups remain unchanged. A manager may return ready() after a state transition to request the next ordered pass.

Test Plan

  • Condition tests verify ready(), after(...), idle(), either(...), deadline expiry, zero delay, and overflow.
  • Request-manager tests verify that request admission and the returned condition agree for in-flight, backoff, missing-coordinator, independent-expiry, completion, and close states. A blocked manager must resume when its required input arrives.
  • Network-loop tests verify one poll per manager, earliest-deadline selection, the existing network-client request-timeout bounds, and the existing application-wait and close behavior. Integration tests exercise the same paths with real network inputs.
  • Performance tests will compare active throughput and idle CPU against a fixed baseline and require no material regression.

Documentation Plan

Internal Javadocs will define each condition, composition rules, deadline handling, and the difference between network and application waiting. Examples will show one manager decision shared by request admission and scheduling, plus an independent expiry.

Rejected Alternatives

Retain the duration-only request-manager model

Request managers can continue returning a scalar duration and repair each busy loop with local guards or a substitute positive timeout. The related application-wait fixes and PR #23357 show that substitute heartbeat, auto-commit, and retry durations may themselves be zero or require an arbitrary floor. Their configured values then control blocked-state polling even though passage of those durations cannot satisfy the blocking prerequisite.

The proposal retains deadline-driven network polling while replacing the duration-only manager result with explicit conditions. For network scheduling, blocked work uses idle() for every timer configuration; eligible work uses ready() or after(...); independent deadlines combine through either(...). The existing application-wait policy remains unchanged.

Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: [DISCUSS] KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers

JIRA: KAFKA-20995

Release: TBD

Summary

The async consumer has repeatedly entered busy loops when a timer reaches zero while another state blocks the related work. The current numeric wait says when to poll again, but it cannot say whether time can make the work eligible or another event must occur first. Existing fixes replace the zero with another duration, which can make correctness depend on that duration's configuration.

This KIP introduces the internal ManagerPollCondition type with ready(), after(...), and idle(). Each request-manager poll() returns its outgoing requests and the condition for the next manager pass. The same manager decision can govern request admission and network scheduling. The network thread combines all manager conditions and applies the existing network-poll bounds. Public APIs, protocols, and thread topology remain unchanged. The internal per-manager RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long) method becomes applicationPollCondition(long); the application-facing ApplicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait() path remains unchanged.

Motivation

The async consumer has repeatedly entered a busy loop when a timer reaches zero while another state prevents the related work from continuing. The loop polls the same request managers, gets the same zero wait, and immediately starts again.

Today, each request manager returns outgoing requests and one numeric wait. The network thread uses the minimum:

java

0 starts another iteration immediately, a finite value schedules a timed iteration, and Long.MAX_VALUE adds no earlier deadline.

The application wait follows the same numeric model. Each manager returns a duration from RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long). The network thread publishes the minimum as cachedMaximumTimeToWait, and the application thread uses it to limit its wait.

Evidence from existing busy-loop fixes

The following issues share the same pattern: work is blocked, but its timer still contributes zero.

Why the current timeout substitutions are incomplete

The fixes repair their reported paths by replacing one zero wait with another duration. PR #22836 and PR #23227 used heartbeat or auto-commit intervals. PR #23348 later used retry backoff because the heartbeat interval starts at zero and auto-commit may be configured as zero. PR #23357 also uses the configured retry backoff while a heartbeat request is in flight.

This approach has three drawbacks:

  • Correctness becomes configuration-dependent. A setting intended to control retry timing also decides whether blocked work enters a busy loop; configuring the replacement timer as zero restores the zero-wait loop.
  • A positive delay only postpones the next poll. Some prerequisites change when an event arrives: a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout resolves an in-flight request, while discovery supplies an unavailable coordinator. If none of these events has occurred, the next poll finds the manager still blocked.
  • A duration does not explain why the manager should run again. When backoff expires, the manager may send a request. When a request is in flight, the same elapsed time changes nothing; the manager still needs a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout.

The fixes remain correct for their reported cases, but they do not define one rule for future request-manager states.

Public consumer classes, metrics, configuration, wire protocols, persisted data, and broker behavior remain unchanged. ManagerPollCondition and the changes to PollResult remain internal to org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.

1. Introduce ManagerPollCondition

This KIP introduces the following internal type for request-manager scheduling:

java

The three factories describe when another manager pass can be useful:

FormMeaningWait returned by remainingMs(...)
ready()Another pass can perform work immediately.Zero
after(now, delayMs)Time can make another pass useful.Time remaining to the retained deadline
idle()This work has no local deadline.Long.MAX_VALUE

The implementation represents ready() and idle() as enum singletons:

java

either(first, second) is ready when either input is ready and retains the earlier wait. Therefore, either(ready(), x) is ready(), either(idle(), x) is x, and two timed conditions retain the earlier deadline instance. The implementation may return that instance directly to avoid allocating a composite.

after(...) rejects negative delays and retains one saturating absolute deadline. Zero delay is valid.

isReady(...) authorizes only the action whose condition was checked. A combined condition may be ready because another action expired while request sending remains blocked.

idle() removes only the deadline for this work. Other manager work, independent deadlines, network completions, application events, cancellation, and shutdown can still start another pass. For example, an in-flight heartbeat includes an idle() send condition and its independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry through either(...).

  2. When can polling this manager again be useful?
